If you ever tried to play arcade games on a 15 kHz tube, you know the work it takes: kernel patches, modelines, emulator settings, and a different recipe for every card. FliperOS ships all of that ready. You write the ISO to a USB stick, install it from a menu drawn for the tube itself, and the games come out with the right picture: true 240p, no stretching, no blur.
What is inside:
• a Linux 6.18 kernel with the 15 kHz patches and Switchres, so AMD Radeon cards with VGA or DVI-I draw the signal natively (Intel and NVIDIA work too, with super resolution modes)
• GroovyMAME, RetroArch, Flycast, Dolphin, PCSX2, Keisho (Sega Model 2 and 3), DuckStation, OpenBOR, Hypseus Singe and more, each opened in the right video mode
• its own frontend, with list, full screen and grid views, plus Attract-Mode, EmulationStation and Pegasus if you prefer them
• a web panel on your phone: pick a game, watch the cabinet live, put the screen and your controller on the OBS stream
• GunCon 2 light gun with a calibration made for the tube, wheels, Bluetooth controllers and arcade panels
• party play between cabinets on the local network, up to 10 players in MAME games
• Pixelcade and ZeDMD LED displays, and two or three CRTs for Darius, Punch-Out!! and Ferrari F355 Challenge
• a ROM filter for MAME by players, buttons and controls, with a download of only the games that pass, and a downloader that fetches the BIOS your games need
• an on-screen menu over any game (hold Start + Down) for filters, scanlines, geometry, colour and volume
• a second disk for the ROMs, BIOS, art and saves, or a Batocera disk used right where it is
• Windows and PC games packed in one file, through Wine and PortProton, with the flicker filter for the tube
• CDs, DVDs and cartridges from a drive or the Open Source Cartridge Reader
• a commercial mode with a coin slot that charges by time played, and a lab mode for remote help
• gamepads that vibrate in the menus, and a low latency mode with 1000 Hz USB and kernel preemption

The Setup covers video, geometry, audio, network, scraper, ROM lists, MAME romset cleaning, controls and latency, all driven by the cabinet’s own joystick, and SSH is on from the first boot for anything else. Every release is tested in a virtual machine and on a real 15 kHz cabinet.

linkedin: I’m building FliperOS, a free and open-source Linux distribution (Ubuntu 24.04) that turns a PC into an arcade cabinet for CRT monitors. Version {version} is out.

The problem: playing arcade games on a real 15 kHz tube normally costs hours of kernel patches, modelines and emulator configuration, and every graphics card needs a different recipe. The result is usually a blurry or stretched picture, or none at all.
What FliperOS does about it:

• Ships a Linux 6.18 kernel with the 15 kHz patches and Switchres, so AMD Radeon cards with VGA or DVI-I output a true 240p signal natively. Intel and NVIDIA work too, with super resolution modes, and DisplayPort or HDMI to VGA converters are supported.

• Bundles GroovyMAME, RetroArch, Flycast, Dolphin, PCSX2, Keisho (Sega Model 2 and 3), DuckStation, OpenBOR and more, each one started with the right video mode, and an own frontend with list, full screen and grid views.
• Replaces the terminal with a setup menu drawn at 320x240 for the tube itself: video, geometry, audio, network, controls, latency and ROM lists, all driven by a joystick or an arcade panel.
• Adds a web panel at fliperos.local to run the cabinet from a phone: pick a game, watch it live, send the screen, the marquee and the controller to OBS, upload games and check the system.
• Links cabinets over the local network for party play, with lockstep for up to 10 players in MAME games.
• Supports GunCon 2 light guns with a calibration for the tube, wheels, Bluetooth controllers, discs and cartridges from the Open Source Cartridge Reader, and LED displays (Pixelcade, ZeDMD).

• Filters a MAME romset by players, buttons and controls and downloads only the games that suit the cabinet, fetches the BIOS each game needs, and can keep everything on a second disk, even a disk that already holds a Batocera library.

• Opens an on-screen menu over any running game (filters, scanlines, geometry, colour, volume), packs Windows and PC games in a single file, and offers a low latency mode with 1000 Hz USB and kernel preemption.

How it is built: the image is generated in Docker from a reproducible recipe, the kernel patches and the setup menu are in the repository, and updates are published as numbered steps that a cabinet applies in order from its own network connection. Every release is tested in a virtual machine and on a real 15 kHz cabinet.
